channel.title: Acme: Tech News
channel.description: Articles about software, publishing and the open web.

item.title: Google contests EU orders to share search data with rivals
item.description: Google is challenging EU orders that would require it to give rival search services anonymized query, click and ranking data and open parts of Android and Gemini to competitors. Google cites privacy and security risks; DuckDuckGo says the Digital Markets Act includes safeguards and that access could restore competition.

item.title: The flood of synthetic podcasts may be a publicity stunt
item.description: Podnews examines claims that one network is releasing thousands of machine-made podcast episodes. The company says it is not a publicity stunt, but its Quiet Please shows are no longer monetized and the operation has rebranded as Liquid Studios, which focuses on transforming existing content.

item.title: Cloudflare's Matthew Prince proposes a new bargain for the web
item.description: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince argues that automated crawlers now account for more than half of web traffic and that publishers need tools to block, admit or charge them. He discusses micropayments, the economics of independent sites and Cloudflare's decision to release its operating-system code.

item.title: Nvidia releases open tools to contain rogue software agents
item.description: Nvidia released OpenShell and Sentry, an openly developed security stack designed to contain software agents and cut them off when they try to escape. The company says the approach could have stopped this summer's Hugging Face breach and is working with Arm, Intel and dozens of partners.

item.title: FTC chair says developers remain responsible for software agents
item.description: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson rejected treating software agents as independent legal actors, arguing that companies should remain liable for what their products do. His position puts old-fashioned accountability at the center of a fast-moving debate over autonomous services, fraud and consumer protection.

item.title: Meta's Charm aims to route around phone gatekeepers
item.description: Meta unveiled Muse Charm, a pocket-watch-size device that gives direct access to its Muse agent without opening a phone app. The move is another attempt to loosen Apple and Google's control over personal computing, but it also asks users to accept a new proprietary hardware-and-service platform.

item.title: Paramount-Warner settlement promises a news-independence board
item.description: Twelve states and the Writers Guild settled challenges to Paramount's $81 billion Warner Bros. Discovery purchase. The terms include a board monitoring editorial independence at CBS and CNN, separate cable negotiations for five years, added U.S. film investment and a worker fund. The merger still concentrates two giant news and entertainment libraries.

item.title: Texas freezes data-center permits pending grid audit
item.description: Gov. Greg Abbott halted new state permits for Texas data centers until regulators audit their electricity, water and tax-incentive impacts. Projects seeking grid connections total more than five times the state's peak demand. The reversal shows how infrastructure costs are moving from a background concern to a direct constraint on the computing boom.

item.title: Cybercrime feud spills into the open after rival site's takeover
item.description: Extortion group ShinyHunters says it exploited a flaw to seize rival cl0p's dark-web site, briefly replacing it with a takeover notice. Researchers told Reuters the clash appears genuine and unusually public. The feud reportedly centers on a stolen Oracle E-Business Suite exploit, showing how software vulnerabilities themselves become contested criminal assets.

item.title: New York and Polymarket trade lawsuits over prediction markets
item.description: New York sued to stop Polymarket from operating as an unlicensed gambling business, arguing that sports and election contracts expose users—including people under 21—to gambling risks. Polymarket answered with a federal suit, saying its exchange falls under federal commodities oversight. The clash tests whether states may regulate prediction markets as gambling.

item.title: WordPress takes the lead at the Open Website Alliance
item.description: Mary Hubbard, executive director of the WordPress Foundation, has become president of the Open Website Alliance. The rotating coalition of WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and TYPO3 advocates for open-source publishing and shares practices across projects, including work on European security rules for community-built content-management systems.

item.title: European software firms reject calls to slow model development
item.description: European software companies are resisting U.S. industry calls to slow advanced-model development, warning that a pause could entrench today's dominant vendors and deepen dependence on American technology. The dispute pits safety concerns and independent evaluation against competition, open alternatives and Europe's push for digital sovereignty.

item.title: Google avoids breakup but faces new ad-tech restrictions
item.description: A federal judge declined to break up Google's advertising business after finding illegal monopoly power, but ordered the company to loosen auction rules, open its ad server to rival exchanges and accept six years of oversight. The remedy matters directly to publishers that depend on the open-web ad market.

item.title: EU tests privacy-minded age checks for the web
item.description: The European Commission is piloting a free, open-source age-verification app in seven countries. Its decentralized design proves that a user meets an age threshold without disclosing identity documents or biometrics to websites, an important test of whether safety rules can avoid creating a universal tracking system.

item.title: Taxpayers funded a TV ad echoing midterm campaign themes
item.description: A 30-second spot airing on Fox News and Newsmax carried presidential imagery and themes used by Republican candidates but disclosed that the U.S. government paid for it. Lawmakers from both parties questioned the use of public money, while the White House called the ad educational and patriotic.
